kurals.tamil:
செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவிக்கு வையகமும்
வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyyaamal seydha udhavikku vaiyagamum
Vaanagamum aatral aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Help given to you when you had done nothing to earn it is so great that even the gift of earth and heaven together could hardly repay it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid you barely know shares their lunch with you on a day you forgot yours, even though you never did anything for them. This kural says a kindness like that is so big that even if you gave them the whole world and the sky too, it still would not be enough to pay it back.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with its most extreme claim. Parimelazhagar reads செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி as help rendered to someone who had done no prior service to the giver: a benefit that is not itself a repayment and therefore springs from pure goodwill. The predicate வையகமும் வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது (earth and heaven can hardly equal it) deliberately places the debt beyond any possible exchange; if the terrestrial and celestial worlds together are inadequate, gratitude cannot be discharged by payment and must become a permanent disposition instead. This anticipates a problem that Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 8.14) and Seneca (De Beneficiis) would both recognise: a class of benefits, above all those from parents and gods, that no return can equal. Placing the chapter in the இல்லறவியல் (householder's section), immediately after Pleasant Speech, frames gratitude as a social virtue that sustains the web of reciprocity on which household and community life depend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That trouble (and pain) which the parents undergo on the birth of (their) children, cannot be compensated even in a hundred years.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that what parents go through to bring a child into the world is a debt so large that a whole century of repayment would not settle it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a kindness that no amount of return can ever balance out.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 2.227 (G. Bühler trans., Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the 'unrepayable debt' idea, but the benefactors are parents, not someone who helps without any prior tie, which is the Kural's specific point.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says God's love is shown by the fact that Christ died for people before they had done anything to deserve it, while they were still in the wrong.
christianity.tie_back: This is the ultimate 'help given when nothing was done to earn it', the exact kind of help the Kural calls beyond repayment.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural match (unearned benefit); the Christian frame is divine grace rather than human gratitude between equals, and the verse does not itself discuss repayment.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who does not thank the people is not thankful to Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a person who fails to thank the humans who help them has not truly thanked God either.
islam.tie_back: It raises gratitude to a human helper to the level of a religious duty, echoing the Kural's claim that such help outweighs heaven and earth.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4811 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Establishes the duty of gratitude to human benefactors, but says nothing about the unrepayable size of unprompted help.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then she fell on her face, and bowed herself to the ground, and said unto him, Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?”
judaism.explanation: Ruth, a poor foreigner gleaning in Boaz's field, bows to the ground in astonishment that a stranger with no obligation to her would show her such kindness.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth's response models the Kural's attitude: overwhelming gratitude for kindness she had not earned from the giver.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good emotional match; however Boaz explains in 2:11 that he acts because of her loyalty to Naomi, so the kindness is not wholly 'unprompted'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If you were to establish your mother & father in absolute sovereignty over this great earth, abounding in the seven treasures, you would not in that way pay or repay your parents.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that even making your parents rulers of the whole earth and all its treasures would not repay what they did for you.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: the entire earth is not enough to repay a great kindness.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.32 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking verbal parallel ('this great earth' cannot repay); the benefactors are parents rather than unrelated helpers, so the 'unprompted' element is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the swineherd Eumaeus welcomes a ragged stranger (Odysseus in disguise) who has never done anything for him, feeds him from his own scanty stock, and says strangers and beggars come from Zeus; Odysseus prays that Zeus grant his host his heart's desire in return.
greek_mythology.explanation: A poor servant freely feeds a beggar he owes nothing to, and the beggar, moved, asks the gods to repay what he himself cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows unprompted kindness whose worth is so great that only the gods can balance it, close to the Kural's heaven-and-earth image.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Primarily a xenia (hospitality) scene; gratitude and repayment are present but the Kural's claim about the incalculable size of the debt is only implied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for no one could ever return to them the equivalent of what he gets, but the man who serves them to the utmost of his power is thought to be a good man.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that with gods and parents we can never pay back an equal amount, so a good person simply does as much as they possibly can.
philosophy.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: some benefits are too large to repay, so gratitude becomes a lifelong attitude rather than a settled account.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.14, 1163b (W. D. Ross trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Explicit 'no equivalent return is possible' claim; restricted to gods and parents rather than unprompted helpers.

kurals.tamil:
காலத்தி னாற்செய்த நன்றி சிறிதெனினும்
ஞாலத்தின் மாணப் பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaalaththinaal seydha nandri siridheninum
Gnaalaththin maanap peridhu.
kurals.meaning: A favour done at the moment of real need, however small in itself, is worth far more than the whole world.
kurals.elementary: If you are thirsty in the middle of a race and someone hands you one small cup of water, that cup feels more valuable than a whole shop full of drinks later. Help that comes right when you need it is the biggest kind of help, even if it is tiny.
kurals.university: The operative word is காலத்தினால், 'by reason of the time', that is, timeliness. Valluvar shifts the measure of a benefit from its quantity (சிறிதெனினும், 'though small') to its moment, and then inflates it past ஞாலம், the whole earth, with the intensifier மாண ('exceedingly'). Kurals 102 to 104 form a graded triad of hyperbolic comparisons (world, sea, palmyra palm), each isolating a different factor that magnifies a benefit: timing, disinterestedness, and the recipient's discernment. The underlying intuition is almost economic: the value of help peaks at the point of greatest need, which is why Solomon Pappaiah glosses the phrase as help given in our time of crisis. Aristotle records the same argument from the benefactor's side, noting that givers insist their help came 'in times of danger or similar need' (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana carries Sita off, the aged vulture-king Jatayu flies at him and fights until he is mortally wounded. Dying, he tells Rama what happened; Rama grieves for him as for his own father and performs his funeral rites with his own hands.
hinduism.explanation: An old bird who could not really win still threw himself into the fight at the exact moment Sita needed help, and Rama honoured that help as if Jatayu were family.
hinduism.tie_back: Jatayu's help was small in outcome but came at the critical hour, and Rama treated it as immeasurably great, just as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 49-51 and 67-68 (sarga numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit for timely help honoured beyond its practical result; the text does not state the 'worth more than the world' evaluation explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus's parable of the judgment, the King counts simple acts like a meal, a drink, or a bed given to someone in need as done to him, with eternal consequences.
christianity.tie_back: Small, timely help given in someone's moment of need is valued far beyond its size, which is the Kural's point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the idea that small help in need carries immense value; framed from the giver's reward rather than the recipient's gratitude.

islam.quote_or_event: “So he (went down the well), filled his shoe with water, caught hold of it with his teeth and climbed up and watered the dog. Allah thanked him for his (good) deed and forgave him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet told of a man who saw a dog dying of thirst, climbed down a well to fill his shoe with water for it, and was forgiven by God for that one small act.
islam.tie_back: A tiny act done at the exact moment of need is treated as enormous, even by God, just as the Kural says timely help outweighs the world.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on small-but-timely help having outsized worth; here the one who 'thanks' is God rather than the recipient.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rashi, following the Midrash, explains that Aaron rather than Moses struck the Nile to begin the plagues, because the river had sheltered Moses when he was placed in it as an infant; Moses would not strike what had once protected him.
judaism.explanation: Even a river that once kept baby Moses safe in his moment of danger was owed gratitude, so Moses would not hit it.
judaism.tie_back: Help given at the critical moment, even by water, earns lasting gratitude, far out of proportion to the 'size' of the act.
judaism.source: Rashi on Exodus 7:19 (drawing on Midrash Tanchuma)
judaism._accuracy_note: Classic Jewish teaching on hakarat hatov for timely help; concerns an inanimate benefactor, so it is illustrative rather than a direct parallel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Pali commentarial biography, in the second week after his awakening the Buddha stood gazing without blinking at the Bodhi tree that had sheltered him during his final struggle; the spot is honoured at Bodh Gaya as the Animisa (Animeshlochana) Cetiya, and later tradition reads the act as gratitude to the tree.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha spent a whole week simply looking at the tree that had given him shade while he struggled for enlightenment.
buddhism.tie_back: Shade is a small gift, but given at the decisive moment it was honoured as something immense, like the Kural's timely favour.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (commentarial biography); Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Bodh Gaya
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: the 'gratitude' interpretation comes from later tradition rather than the canonical suttas; used as the best available narrative parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Aesopic fable of the Ant and the Dove, an ant falls into a stream and is drowning when a dove drops a leaf or twig beside it, letting it climb to safety; later the ant stings a bird-catcher's foot just as he is about to snare the dove.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leaf is almost nothing, but dropped at the exact moment the ant was drowning it saved its life, and the ant never forgot it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A tiny, timely favour is repaid as if it were enormous, which is the Kural's lesson.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Ant and the Dove (Perry Index 235; G. F. Townsend trans.)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Aesopic fable rather than myth proper, but a clean illustration of small help at the critical moment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that a benefit given promptly, before it has to be asked for, is received with far greater gratitude, while one that is delayed or extracted by long pleading loses much of its value; hesitation, he says, is close to refusal.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman Stoic says the same gift is worth more when it comes quickly, right when needed, than when it arrives late.
philosophy.tie_back: Timing multiplies the worth of a favour, exactly the variable the Kural isolates.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Seneca speaks mainly to the giver's promptness, whereas the Kural speaks to the recipient's valuation; the principle is shared.

kurals.tamil:
பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி நயன்தூக்கின்
நன்மை கடலின் பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Payandhookkaar seydha udhavi nayandhookkin
Nanmai kadalin peridhu.
kurals.meaning: When someone helps without calculating what they will get back, the goodness of that help, if you truly weigh it, is greater than the ocean.
kurals.elementary: Some people help you because they want something later, like a sticker trade. Others help just because they care. This kural says the second kind of help is bigger than the whole sea.
kurals.university: The couplet hinges on a pun on தூக்கு, 'to weigh': the benefactor is பயன்தூக்கார், one who does not weigh the return, while the recipient is invited to weigh (நயன்தூக்கின்) the help's goodness or love (நயன், from நயம்). Gratitude is thus framed as an act of moral appraisal that the giver refused to perform on his own behalf; the asymmetry is the point. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss நயன் as the love (அன்பு) behind the act, so the 'sea' measures not the material help but the disinterested affection it expresses. This parallels the Bhagavad Gita's category of sattvic giving (17.20), made 'without expectation of return', and Aristotle's remark (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13) that it is noble to benefit another without a view to repayment even though most people prefer to receive. The kural quietly criticises transactional benevolence while insisting that recipients never take pure generosity lightly.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the highest, purest kind of giving is giving that expects nothing back.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita praises exactly the kind of help the Kural says is 'vaster than the sea': help given without weighing the return.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match on 'without expectation of return' (anupakarine); the Gita speaks from the giver's side, while the Kural speaks to the recipient's gratitude.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to do good and lend without hoping to get anything back, because that is how God himself behaves.
christianity.tie_back: 'Hoping for nothing again' is the Kural's பயன்தூக்கார், the one who does not weigh the return.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on disinterested giving; the verse even mentions the 'unthankful', but it is addressed to givers rather than recipients.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], “We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the righteous feeding the poor, the orphan and the captive while telling them they want neither payment nor even thanks, only God's pleasure.
islam.tie_back: This is the purest form of help 'that does not weigh the return', whose worth the Kural calls greater than the sea.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match: explicit renunciation of any return, even of gratitude; again framed from the giver's side.

judaism.quote_or_event: Commenting on Jacob's request that Joseph bury him in Canaan, Rashi explains that kindness done for the dead is called chesed shel emet, 'true kindness', because the one who does it expects no repayment.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition says the truest kindness is the kind you do for someone who can never pay you back, like caring for the dead.
judaism.tie_back: Judaism, like the Kural, ranks help that cannot be repaid or calculated as the highest and most precious form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear conceptual match on disinterested kindness; the Kural's recipient-side 'weighing' is not addressed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Diamond Sutra teaches that a bodhisattva should practise giving without being supported by any notion (of self, recipient, gift, or reward), and that the merit of such giving is as immeasurable as space in every direction.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching says the best giving is done without thinking 'I am giving' or 'what will I get', and that such giving is too vast to measure.
buddhism.tie_back: Its 'immeasurable as space' matches the Kural's 'greater than the sea' for help given without calculation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Mahayana metaphysical frame (non-attachment to signs) differs from the Kural's ethical frame, but the vastness image and non-calculating giving line up.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome two unknown travellers (Jupiter and Mercury in disguise) whom richer households had turned away, and share their meagre food with no hope of return; the gods reward them by turning their hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: A very poor couple shared everything they had with strangers without expecting anything back, and the gods counted that kindness as enormous.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hospitality given without weighing any return is judged immensely great, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.618-724 (Roman retelling of a Phrygian legend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for disinterested giving; the source is a Latin poet's treatment of a Greek-world myth, and gratitude here flows from gods to humans.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “now it is noble to do well by another without a view to repayment, but it is the receiving of benefits that is advantageous.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that helping without expecting repayment is the noble thing, even though most people would rather be on the receiving end.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle names the same 'not weighing the return' that the Kural says makes help vaster than the sea.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.13, 1162b (W. D. Ross trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-direct conceptual parallel; Aristotle goes on to say the recipient should still repay if possible, which fits the chapter as a whole.

kurals.tamil:
தினைத்துணை நன்றி செயினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பயன்தெரி வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thinaiththunai nandri seyinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar payantheri vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who understand the value of kindness treat a favour as small as a millet seed as if it were as tall as a palm tree.
kurals.elementary: A millet seed is tiny, smaller than a grain of rice. A palm tree is huge. A grateful person takes even a tiny kindness, like someone lending a pencil, and treats it like something huge.
kurals.university: தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains in the Tamil diet) and பனை (the palmyra, the tallest and most useful tree of the Tamil landscape) form one of the Kural's most memorable scale contrasts; the same pair recurs in Kural 433, where those who fear disgrace treat a fault the size of millet as if it were the size of a palm. The subject பயன்தெரிவார், 'those who discern the fruit or benefit', makes gratitude a cognitive virtue: the grateful person perceives consequences that the literal size of the gift conceals. Kalaignar's gloss exploits the palmyra's many uses (fruit, leaf, timber, sap) to suggest that a small help ramifies into manifold benefit. The same inversion of scale appears in the Gospel's widow's mite, in the Talmud's 'good guest' of Berakhot 58a, and in Seneca's argument that a benefit lies in the intention rather than in the object given.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I will accept it.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says he gladly accepts even a single leaf or a little water when it is offered with love, treating the tiny gift as precious.
hinduism.tie_back: The One who needs nothing treats the smallest offering as great, the same 'millet seen as palm' attitude the Kural praises (compare Krishna's welcome of Sudama's handful of rice in the Bhagavata Purana).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Captures the valuing of small gifts by their spirit; it is God receiving worship rather than a human recipient showing gratitude.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus watches a poor widow drop two tiny coins into the temple box and says she gave more than all the rich donors.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus sees a millet-sized gift as palm-sized because he looks at what it really means, just like the discerning people in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Excellent match on revaluing a small gift; the context is almsgiving to the Temple rather than gratitude for a favour received.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that even the tiniest good deed, the weight of an atom, is noticed and counts on the Day of Judgment.
islam.tie_back: No good deed is too small to matter; the Kural asks the grateful person to see small kindnesses with that same attention.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the 'nothing is too small' principle, but concerns divine accounting of deeds rather than a recipient magnifying a favour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good guest, what does he say? How much effort did the host expend on my behalf, how much meat did the host bring before me.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud contrasts a good guest, who counts up everything the host did for him, with a bad guest, who says he only ate one piece of bread and the host did it all for his own family anyway.
judaism.tie_back: The good guest is exactly the Kural's பயன்தெரிவார்: someone who sees a modest meal as a great kindness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: the grateful recipient magnifies the benefactor's effort while the ungrateful one minimises it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada commentary tells of Radha, a poor old brahmin whom no monk would ordain. The Buddha asked whether anyone remembered a kindness from him; Sariputta recalled that Radha had once given him a single ladleful of rice, and out of gratitude he ordained and trained Radha, who became an arahant. The Buddha praised Sariputta's gratitude.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's chief disciple remembered that a poor man had once given him one spoonful of rice, and repaid it by becoming his teacher.
buddhism.tie_back: One ladle of rice treated as a debt worth years of teaching is a perfect 'millet seen as a palm tree'.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 76 (Radha Thera story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match (tiny gift, huge grateful return); the source is the commentarial tradition, not the canonical verse itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Aesopic fable of the Lion and the Mouse, a lion scoffs at a mouse's promise to repay him for sparing its life, but when the lion is later caught in a hunter's net the mouse gnaws through the ropes and frees him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lion thought a mouse could never help him, but the little creature's small help ended up saving the king of beasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It teaches, like the Kural, that small help can be enormous in value to those wise enough to see it.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (Perry Index 150; G. F. Townsend trans.)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fable rather than myth; it shows small help proving great, but the lion is corrected by events rather than showing discerning gratitude from the start.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that a benefit does not consist in the thing given (money, a meal, an office) but in the goodwill of the giver, so a small gift given with a good heart can be a greater benefit than a lavish one.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic says what makes a favour great is the kind intention behind it, not how much it costs.
philosophy.tie_back: Those who 'know the value' in the Kural look past the millet seed's size to the goodwill it carries.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match; Seneca locates value in intention, while the Kural stresses the recipient's discernment of the gift's fruit (பயன்).

kurals.tamil:
உதவி வரைத்தன்று உதவி உதவி
செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Udhavi varaiththandru udhavi udhavi
Seyappattaar saalbin varaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The worth of a favour is not set by the favour itself; it is set by the character of the person who received it.
kurals.elementary: If a friend gives you a small gift, how much you give back is not just about the size of their gift. It is about what kind of person you are. A really good-hearted person gives back even more than they got.
kurals.university: Built on a fourfold repetition of உதவி (help), the couplet admits two readings. Parimelazhagar, followed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, takes the first உதவி as the return-favour: requital is not bounded by the size of the original help but by the சால்பு (nobility, fullness of character) of the one who was helped, so a noble recipient repays abundantly. Kalaignar reads it evaluatively: the value of a help is assessed according to the recipient's worth. Both readings converge on the claim that gratitude measures the recipient rather than balancing a ledger, linking this chapter to the later chapter on சான்றாண்மை (perfect character). Aristotle frames the same dispute, whether to measure a service by its utility to the receiver or by the benevolence of the giver (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13), and Cicero, citing Hesiod, urges us to imitate fertile fields that return more than they receive (De Officiis 1.48).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna's poor boyhood friend Sudama visits him bringing only a handful of flattened rice. Krishna eats it with delight, and Sudama returns home to find his hut transformed into a palace; the return is measured by Krishna's greatness, not by the rice.
hinduism.explanation: A poor friend gave Krishna a tiny gift, and Krishna repaid it with far more than it was 'worth' because of who Krishna is.
hinduism.tie_back: The repayment matched the giver-back's own greatness, not the size of the help, which is the Kural's point about சால்பு.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear narrative match for requital measured by the recipient's nobility; the recipient here is divine, which heightens the point beyond ordinary ethics.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that generosity returns in overflowing measure, pressed down and running over.
christianity.tie_back: The return is not limited to the original amount but overflows, much as the Kural says a noble recipient's requital is not bounded by the original help.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the 'return exceeds the gift' image, but it is a promise about divine and social reciprocity, not about the recipient's character setting the measure.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet [in return] with one better than it or [at least] return it [in a like manner]. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, an Accountant.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to answer a greeting with a better one, or at least an equal one.
islam.tie_back: A good person's response is set by their own goodness and aims higher than what they received, the Kural's standard for repaying help.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear 'return with better' principle; applied to greetings, it is extended by commentators to all courtesies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he said unto his daughters, And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread.”
judaism.explanation: When the fugitive Moses drove off shepherds who were bullying Jethro's daughters at a well, Jethro scolded them for not bringing the stranger home; he took Moses in and later gave him his daughter in marriage.
judaism.tie_back: One act of help at a well was repaid with a home and a family, a return set by Jethro's generosity rather than by the size of the favour.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good narrative illustration of generous requital; the verse itself does not state the principle, which is inferred from the story.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person of integrity is grateful & thankful. This gratitude, this thankfulness, is advocated by civil people. It is entirely on the level of people of integrity.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that gratitude is what marks a person of integrity, while ingratitude marks a person without it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the way we respond to help a measure of our own character.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.31 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on gratitude as a measure of the recipient's worth; it does not discuss the size of the requital.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises taking fair measure from a neighbour and paying it back fairly with the same measure, or better if you are able, so that you may find him reliable when you are in need again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The old Greek poet tells farmers to repay what a neighbour lent them with at least as much, and more if they can.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Repaying 'better if you can' makes the requital depend on the character and ability of the recipient, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 349-351 (H. G. Evelyn-White trans.)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Archaic Greek didactic poetry rather than myth narrative; the principle of generous requital is a close fit, though its motive is partly prudential.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But if, as Hesiod bids, one is to repay with interest, if possible, what one has borrowed in time of need, what, pray, ought we to do when challenged by an unsought kindness? Shall we not imitate the fruitful fields, which return more than they receive?”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says that if we repay loans with interest, we should repay an unasked-for kindness even more generously, like good soil that gives back more than was sown.
philosophy.tie_back: A good person's requital overflows the original favour, just as the Kural says it is measured by the recipient's nobility.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 1.48 (Walter Miller trans., Loeb 1913)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close: explicit 'return more than received' plus the 'unsought kindness' of Kural 101; Cicero grounds it in duty rather than in the recipient's character as such.

kurals.tamil:
மறவற்க மாசற்றார் கேண்மை துறவற்க
துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Maravarka maasatraar kenmai thuravarka
Thunbaththul thuppaayaar natpu.
kurals.meaning: Never forget the friendship of people who are pure-hearted, and never abandon the friendship of those who stood by you as your strength in hard times.
kurals.elementary: Some friends are simply good people, so don't forget them. And some friends helped you when you were sad or in trouble, so never walk away from them, even after things get better for you.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as two parallel prohibitions, மறவற்க ('do not forget') and துறவற்க ('do not forsake'), each governing a class of relationship: the கேண்மை (bond) of the மாசற்றார் (the stainless) and the நட்பு (friendship) of those who became துப்பு (strength, support) in துன்பம் (distress). Commentators take the first half to concern those free of fault in knowledge and conduct and the second those who helped in adversity; the chapter thereby widens gratitude from discrete favours to durable relationships. The verb துறத்தல், the same root used for renunciation, suggests that abandoning a former helper is a kind of moral apostasy. The theme anticipates the Kural's later friendship chapters (79-83), where adversity is repeatedly named as the true test of a friend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, when Krishna reveals to Karna that he is Kunti's eldest son and offers him the throne if he joins the Pandavas, Karna refuses: Duryodhana had honoured and befriended him when others scorned his low birth, and he will not abandon that friend on the eve of war.
hinduism.explanation: Karna turns down a kingdom because he will not desert the friend who stood by him when everyone else looked down on him.
hinduism.tie_back: Karna lives out the Kural's command: never forsake the friendship of one who was your support in your time of humiliation.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Karna's reply to Krishna; K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong narrative match for loyalty to one who helped in adversity; complicated by the fact that Duryodhana is the epic's antagonist, so the loyalty is tragic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:”
christianity.explanation: From prison, Paul blesses the family of Onesiphorus, who kept visiting and comforting him and was not ashamed to be seen with a prisoner.
christianity.tie_back: Paul refuses to forget the friend who stood by him 'in his chains', the exact friend the Kural says never to forsake.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct match: grateful remembrance of a friend who supported one in adversity.

islam.quote_or_event: Aisha reported that, years after Khadijah's death, the Prophet mentioned her very often and, whenever he slaughtered a sheep, sent portions to Khadijah's women friends; when Aisha objected, he would reply by recalling what Khadijah had been to him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet kept honouring his first wife Khadijah, who had supported him from the very beginning, long after she died, even sending gifts to her friends.
islam.tie_back: He never forgot or let go of the bond with the one who had been his strength in the hardest early years, as the Kural commands.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on lasting loyalty; this hadith does not itself mention her support in adversity (that detail comes from other reports, e.g. in Musnad Ahmad).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother’s house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells us never to abandon an old friend, or a friend of the family, and says a friend close by in trouble is worth more than a distant relative.
judaism.tie_back: 'Forsake not' is the Kural's துறவற்க, applied to the friend who is near in calamity.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close verbal and conceptual match ('forsake not' friends, value of help in calamity).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “in misfortune he does not forsake one,”
buddhism.explanation: In advice to the layman Sigala, the Buddha lists the marks of a true friend, including that he does not abandon you when misfortune strikes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha defines a real friend by the same test the Kural uses: staying with you in hard times.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (Narada Thera trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Describes what a good friend does rather than commanding the helped person not to forsake such a friend; the two are mirror images.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Heracles, after the hero has killed his own wife and children in a god-sent madness, Theseus arrives, recalls that Heracles once rescued him from the underworld, refuses to shun him as polluted, and offers him a home and honours in Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: When everyone else would run from Heracles after his terrible disaster, Theseus stands by him because Heracles had once saved him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Theseus refuses to abandon the friend who had been his rescuer, embodying both halves of the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Heracles (c. 416 BCE), the Theseus episode
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent match: gratitude for past rescue expressed as loyalty in the benefactor's own catastrophe.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On Friendship, Cicero quotes Ennius's line that a sure friend is discerned in an unsure situation, and argues that people who desert friends in adversity, or who grow proud in prosperity, show themselves unfit for true friendship.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says you only really find out who your friends are when things go wrong, and that leaving a friend in trouble shows weak character.
philosophy.tie_back: He makes adversity the test of friendship, the same test behind the Kural's 'do not forsake'.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on adversity as the test of friendship; less focused on gratitude for help received.

kurals.tamil:
எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர் தங்கண்
விழுமந் துடைத்தவர் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ezhumai ezhupirappum ulluvar thangan
Vizhuman thudaiththavar natpu.
kurals.meaning: The good remember, through all their seven births, the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
kurals.elementary: If someone wiped away your tears when you were really hurting, you should remember them for a very, very long time. The kural says: for seven whole lifetimes!
kurals.university: விழுமம் denotes grave affliction, and துடைத்தல், 'to wipe away', evokes the wiping of tears, an image that G. U. Pope's verse translation foregrounds. எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் is variously parsed: traditional commentary reads it within the South Asian doctrine of rebirth as 'through sevenfold births', while modern commentators such as Kalaignar treat it as hyperbole meaning 'without any limit of time'. Either way, the couplet turns gratitude from a transaction into a form of memory (உள்ளுவர், 'they will keep in mind') whose duration exceeds a single life. The motif of long-lived or even inherited gratitude, such as David's kindness to Jonathan's son, Rama's avowed debt to Hanuman, and the Buddha's thought of the five companions after his awakening, shows how widely traditions have treated rescuers as creditors whose claim outlives the moment of rescue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda, as Hanuman takes leave, Rama tells him that he would give his life for each single service Hanuman has done and still remain in his debt, and that he wishes these favours to stay unrepaid within him, since a return is needed only when a benefactor falls into misfortune.
hinduism.explanation: Rama tells Hanuman he can never finish repaying him, and even hopes he never gets the chance, because that would mean Hanuman was in trouble.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama's gratitude to the one who wiped away his sorrow is lifelong and open-ended, just like the Kural's 'seven births'.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Rama's farewell to Hanuman; chapter numbering varies by edition, commonly 7.40)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit (unending debt to a rescuer); paraphrased because chapter numbering and wording differ across editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I thank my God upon every remembrance of you,”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church at Philippi, which had supported him from the start, that every time he remembers them he thanks God.
christianity.tie_back: Gratitude that returns with every memory is the Kural's 'they will keep in mind', applied to those who helped in hardship.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches ongoing grateful remembrance; the 'lifetimes' hyperbole and the specific image of wiping away sorrow are absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, “My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small.””
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to be humble to their aged parents and to pray for them, remembering how they cared for them as little children.
islam.tie_back: Gratitude here reaches back across a whole lifetime to care received long ago, like the Kural's unending remembrance.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures lifelong remembrance of care; limited to parents rather than any friend who relieved one's distress.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
judaism.explanation: After his friend Jonathan died, King David searched for any surviving relative so he could repay Jonathan's friendship, and found and cared for Jonathan's disabled son Mephibosheth.
judaism.tie_back: David's gratitude to the friend who protected him outlived the friend himself, the kind of remembrance the Kural stretches across 'seven births'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match: gratitude to a friend who saved one's life, extended beyond that friend's death to the next generation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, when the Buddha considered whom to teach first, he thought of his former teachers Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta (both had died), and then of the group of five monks who had attended him during his years of striving, recalling that they had been very helpful to him.
buddhism.explanation: The first people the newly enlightened Buddha wanted to share his discovery with were those who had helped him through his hardest years.
buddhism.tie_back: Even at the moment of enlightenment, the Buddha's mind turned first to those who had eased his hardships, as the Kural says the good always do.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit for remembered help during hardship; the sutta frames it as the choice of who could understand the teaching, with gratitude implicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Odysseus leaves Phaeacia, the princess Nausicaa, who found him naked and shipwrecked on the shore and brought him to safety, asks him to remember her, since he owes her his life; Odysseus answers that if he reaches home he will pray to her as to a goddess all his days.
greek_mythology.explanation: The young princess who rescued Odysseus from his worst moment asks him not to forget her, and he promises to honour her for the rest of his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Lifelong remembrance of the one who ended your affliction is exactly the Kural's teaching.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on lifelong gratitude to a rescuer; the rebirth dimension of 'seven births' has no Homeric equivalent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius opens his Meditations with an entire book listing, person by person, what he owes to his grandfather, mother, teachers, friends, his adoptive father Antoninus, and the gods, naming the specific good each gave him.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman emperor began his private notebook by writing down everyone who had helped him become who he was, and exactly how.
philosophy.tie_back: Book 1 is a written act of the long remembrance the Kural prescribes: keeping benefactors in mind across a whole life.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on deliberate lifelong remembrance of benefactors; not specific to those who relieved affliction.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றி மறப்பது நன்றன்று நன்றல்லது
அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandri marappadhu nandrandru nandralladhu
Andre marappadhu nandru.
kurals.meaning: It is not good to forget a kindness done to you; but it is good to forget a wrong done to you on the very same day.
kurals.elementary: Keep the good things people do for you in your memory box forever. But if someone is mean to you, try to let it go before you go to bed that night.
kurals.university: The couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar's wordplay, circling the root நன்று (good) through நன்றி (a benefit), நன்றன்று (not good) and நன்றல்லது (what is not good, i.e. an injury), and pivoting on அன்றே, 'that very day'. It proposes an asymmetric economy of memory: benefits are to be retained indefinitely, injuries released at once. Ethically, this protects gratitude from being eroded by later grievances, a theme the next couplet (109) develops; psychologically, it anticipates modern research that treats gratitude and forgiveness as complementary dispositions. The instruction to let go of a wrong 'that very day' closely parallels Ephesians 4:26 ('let not the sun go down upon your wrath'), while the Psalmist's 'forget not all his benefits' supplies the other half of the Kural's pairing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Ravana's defeat, Hanuman offers to punish the demon women who had tormented Sita during her captivity, but Sita forbids it, saying they only acted under orders, that a noble person shows compassion even to wrongdoers, and that there is no one who never errs.
hinduism.explanation: Sita refuses revenge on the guards who frightened and bullied her for months and lets the wrong go as soon as she is free.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita forgets the injury immediately, the second half of the Kural's teaching.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Hanuman's report to Sita; commonly sarga 113-116 depending on edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on forgiving injury; does not address remembering benefits, so it matches only half of the couplet.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says anger itself may happen, but you should not let it last past sunset.
christianity.tie_back: 'Not letting the sun go down' is almost exactly the Kural's 'forget it that very day' (அன்றே).
christianity._accuracy_note: Striking parallel on the same-day release of grievance; the gratitude half of the couplet is not addressed.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give [aid] to their relatives and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allah, and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: Revealed, according to the commentators, when Abu Bakr vowed to stop supporting a relative who had joined in slandering his daughter Aisha, the verse told him to pardon, overlook, and keep giving.
islam.tie_back: It tells the believer to drop the injury rather than let it cancel the relationship of kindness, the Kural's balance of forgetting wrongs and keeping goodness alive.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear match on forgiving injury; here the forgiver is the benefactor rather than the beneficiary, so the gratitude half is inverted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist tells his own soul to praise God and never forget any of the good things God has done.
judaism.tie_back: 'Forget not all his benefits' is the Kural's first half, நன்றி மறப்பது நன்றன்று; Leviticus 19:18's ban on bearing a grudge supplies the second.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-verbal match for not forgetting benefits; directed to God rather than human benefactors, and the forgetting-injury half comes from a different verse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that people who stop replaying the wrongs done to them are the ones whose hatred fades.
buddhism.tie_back: Not harbouring the memory of injury is the Kural's 'forget the wrong'.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on releasing injury; does not address remembering benefits or the 'same day' immediacy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles ends his long wrath against Agamemnon, telling the assembled Achaeans that they should let what is past be past, painful as it was, and master the anger in their hearts.
greek_mythology.explanation: After nursing his grudge for most of the war, Achilles finally decides to let it go.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the release of an injury that the Kural recommends, though Achilles gets there far too late.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak: Achilles lets go only after catastrophe and mainly to avenge Patroclus; it is a counter-example to 'same day' forgetting as much as an example.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that of all the ungrateful, the most ungrateful is the one who has forgotten a benefit, since someone who has let it slip from memory has clearly never thought about repaying it.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic says that forgetting a kindness is the worst kind of ingratitude, because it shows you never even tried to pay it back.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half, 'forgetting a benefit is not good', stated as philosophy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on the gravity of forgetting benefits; the forgiveness half of the Kural is not part of this passage.

kurals.tamil:
கொன்றன்ன இன்னா செயினும் அவர்செய்த
ஒன்றுநன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kondranna innaa seyinum avarseydha
Ondrunandru ullak kedum.
kurals.meaning: Even if someone who once helped you later hurts you as badly as if they had killed you, that hurt fades the moment you remember the one good thing they did.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a friend who once caught you when you were falling later does something that really hurts you. If you remember the time they caught you, the hurt shrinks. One good memory can melt a big hurt.
kurals.university: கொன்றன்ன இன்னா, 'an injury like killing', is the strongest possible provocation, and the verb கெடும் ('will perish') leaves its subject implicit: commentators take it to be the injury, or the pain and resentment it causes, that is destroyed merely by recalling (உள்ள) one (ஒன்று) earlier good (நன்று). The kural thus makes gratitude an active remedy rather than merely a debt: memory of a past benefit is prescribed as the means of dissolving present grievance. Valmiki's portrait of Rama in Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11, gladdened by a single good deed and forgetting a hundred wrongs, is close enough to suggest a shared South Asian ethical ideal. A concrete legal-historical parallel is the Prophet Muhammad's pardon of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, whose betrayal was weighed against his earlier service at Badr.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That Rama, because of his good bent of mind, feels glad even by whatever way a good thing is done to him. He does not remember any number of bad things done to him.”
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki describes Rama as someone who is made happy by even one good thing done for him and simply does not keep count of the wrongs done to him.
hinduism.tie_back: One remembered good cancelling many injuries is the very mechanism of this Kural.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11 (K. M. K. Murthy trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (Sanskrit: pleased by one kindness, does not remember even a hundred injuries); described as a trait of Rama rather than a general precept.

christianity.quote_or_event: After Peter had three times denied knowing Jesus on the night of his arrest, the risen Jesus meets him by the Sea of Galilee, asks him three times whether he loves him, and restores him with the charge to feed his sheep.
christianity.explanation: Instead of punishing Peter for his betrayal, Jesus remembers Peter's love and loyalty and gives him back his place.
christianity.tie_back: A painful betrayal is overcome by recalling the good bond that came before it, close to the Kural's remedy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Moderate: the restoration rests on love and grace rather than explicitly on remembering Peter's past service.

islam.quote_or_event: When Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a was caught sending a secret letter warning the Meccans of the Prophet's plans, Umar asked permission to execute him as a traitor; the Prophet refused, saying that Hatib had fought at Badr and that God may have looked upon the people of Badr and forgiven them.
islam.explanation: A companion committed a serious betrayal that could have cost lives, but the Prophet pardoned him because of the great service he had once given at the Battle of Badr.
islam.tie_back: One remembered good (Badr) outweighed an injury as grave as treason, exactly the Kural's teaching.
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent structural match: a benefactor's later grave offence set aside by recalling his earlier service.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.”
judaism.explanation: Even though Egypt later enslaved and oppressed the Israelites, the Torah forbids hating Egyptians, because Egypt once gave Jacob's family refuge in a famine.
judaism.tie_back: The earlier good (shelter) outweighs even the later near-deadly harm (slavery), precisely the Kural's teaching.
judaism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close: rabbinic tradition reads this verse as hakarat hatov that survives later persecution.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that you can never end hatred by hating back; only letting go of hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it seeks to dissolve the pain of injury inwardly rather than answer it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the aim of dissolving resentment, but offers non-hatred rather than the memory of a past benefit as the means.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: During the slaughter of the suitors, Telemachus begs Odysseus to spare the herald Medon, who had served in the suitors' company but had cared for Telemachus when he was a child; Odysseus spares him, along with the bard Phemius.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the middle of his revenge, Odysseus lets one of the suitors' servants live because that man had once looked after his son.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An old kindness saves a man even when he stands on the side of those who did deadly harm, echoing the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of past good cancelling present guilt; Medon's own offence is association rather than a grave personal injury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a person who lives by the guidance of reason tries, as far as possible, to repay another's hatred, anger, or contempt with love or nobleness, because hatred answered with hatred only increases.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher says a reasonable person answers hurt with kindness instead of revenge, since revenge just makes hatred grow.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts aim to neutralise injury rather than retaliate, though the Kural's method is remembering a past kindness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the goal of overcoming injury without retaliation; lacks the specific mechanism of recalling the injurer's earlier benefit.

kurals.tamil:
எந்நன்றி கொன்றார்க்கும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்வில்லை
செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ennandri kondraarkkum uyvundaam uyvillai
Seynnandri kondra magarku.
kurals.meaning: Those who have destroyed any other virtue may still find a way to be saved, but there is no salvation for the one who destroys gratitude for a kindness done to him.
kurals.elementary: People can make lots of mistakes and still fix them. But this kural says the one thing that is almost impossible to fix is being ungrateful to someone who helped you, so that is the one mistake you should never make.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with its severest verdict. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, following the traditional commentary, read the first நன்றி as அறம் in general ('whoever has killed any virtue'), against which செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகன், the man who has 'killed' a benefit by forgetting it or returning harm for it, stands uniquely without உய்வு (escape, deliverance). The idea has deep roots in Tamil and Sanskrit tradition: the Sangam anthology Puranānūru (poem 34) is commonly cited alongside this kural for declaring that there is no escape for those who destroy a benefit, and Valmiki's Kishkindha Kanda (4.34.12) says atonement is ordained for cow-slayers, drinkers, thieves and vow-breakers but not for the kṛtaghna, the ingrate. Outside South Asia, Cicero held that no duty is more imperative than proving one's gratitude (De Officiis 1.47), and Hume chose ingratitude as the most horrid and unnatural of crimes (Treatise 3.1.1). This agreement suggests that ingratitude was treated not as one vice among many but as the destruction of the reciprocity on which moral community rests.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The savants have ordained atonement for slayers of cows, for drinkers of liquors, thus for thieves and infringers of solemnity, but no atonement is available to a treacherous person.”
hinduism.explanation: Lakshmana, rebuking Sugriva for forgetting his promise to Rama, quotes an old verse: even killers, drunkards and thieves can atone, but there is no atonement for someone who is ungrateful (kṛtaghna, rendered 'treacherous' by this translator).
hinduism.tie_back: Almost word-for-word the Kural's claim: every other sinner has a way out, but the ingrate has none.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 4.34.12 (Desiraju Hanumanta Rao trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical structure: a list of expiable grave sins set against the inexpiable sin of kṛtaghnatā; the translator's 'treacherous' renders kṛtaghna ('one who destroys what was done for him').

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus answering said, Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? There are not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan foreigner, comes back to thank him, and Jesus asks sadly where the other nine are.
christianity.tie_back: The story singles out ingratitude after a life-changing kindness as something that grieves even Jesus.
christianity._accuracy_note: Highlights ingratitude, but does not claim it is uniquely beyond forgiveness as the Kural does.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe.'”
islam.explanation: God promises more blessings to the grateful and warns of severe punishment for those who deny His favours.
islam.tie_back: Ingratitude (kufr of blessings) carries grave consequences, echoing the Kural's warning that it has no escape.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the gravity of ingratitude; addressed to gratitude toward God, and does not rank it as uniquely unforgivable.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that anyone who repays good with evil will never be free of trouble in their household.
judaism.tie_back: 'Evil shall not depart' is a close match for the Kural's 'there is no escape' for the one who kills a kindness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: returning evil for good brings inescapable consequences; lacks the explicit comparison with other sins.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Silavanaga Jataka, the Bodhisatta, born as a noble elephant, rescues a lost forester and carries him to safety. The man returns three times to saw off the elephant's tusks, which are freely given; on his way home the third time the earth splits open and swallows him.
buddhism.explanation: A man keeps taking the tusks of the elephant that saved his life, and after his third betrayal the ground itself opens and swallows him.
buddhism.tie_back: The ingrate who repays rescue with injury meets a doom from which there is no escape, the Kural's verdict told as a story.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 72, Silavanaga Jataka (E. B. Cowell ed., vol. 1)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match for the inescapable fate of the ingrate; a birth-story rather than a doctrinal statement.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how Ixion, whom Zeus had purified and received as a guest among the gods, tried to seduce Hera; bound forever to a winged, turning wheel, he proclaims to mortals that they must repay a benefactor with kind returns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion was forgiven and welcomed by Zeus, then betrayed him, and was punished for all eternity as a warning to everyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is Greek myth's model ingrate, and his punishment is endless, the Kural's 'no escape'.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent match: Pindar explicitly draws the moral of repaying benefactors from Ixion's eternal punishment; paraphrased because the English wording could not be verified online.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all crimes that human creatures are capable of committing, the most horrid and unnatural is ingratitude, especially when it is committed against parents, and appears in the more flagrant instances of wounds and death.”
philosophy.explanation: The Scottish philosopher David Hume uses ingratitude as his example of the crime everyone agrees is the worst, especially ingratitude toward parents.
philosophy.tie_back: Hume ranks ingratitude at the very top of human crimes, matching the Kural's claim that it alone has no escape.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 3.1.1.24
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on ranking; Hume invokes it as a test case for his theory that moral judgments rest on sentiment, not to argue its inexpiability.
